title: Structural Recovery Information Theory: A New Principle for Preserving Cellular Organizational Information and Reconstructing the Functional State
content: How does a cell preserve information about its own organization that is required to reconstruct a functional state after reversible cessation of activity? This question extends beyond the traditional view of cellular survival as the preservation of molecular components. Cellular recoverability depends not only on the preservation of proteins, membranes, DNA, and organelles, but also on the preservation of organizational information that determines how these components must be spatially, structurally, and functionally reassembled after the cell exits a stabilized or metabolically suppressed state. Here, we develop Structural Recovery Information Theory (SRIT), a new conceptual theory proposing that cells preserve not only molecular information but also information about the relationships among molecular components that maintain the possibility of subsequent functional reconstruction. The central concept of SRIT is Structural Recovery Information (SRI), defined as a distributed informational property of cellular organization that determines or constrains possible trajectories of recovery following reversible physiological or metabolic arrest. Unlike genetic, epigenetic, transcriptional, and stress memory, SRI is neither a molecule nor a discrete structure or localized information carrier; rather, it may be instantiated through organelle positioning, membrane architecture, macromolecular complexes, protein–protein interactions, phase-separated condensates, cytoskeletal organization, proteostasis, local metabolite concentrations, molecular crowding, and the physical state of the cytoplasm. Thus, whereas modern biology has traditionally conceptualized biological information primarily through the DNA → RNA → protein paradigm, SRIT extends this view by emphasizing that cellular function depends on the integrated organization of molecules, spatial relationships, interactions, phase state, topology, and dynamics. The theory distinguishes cellular viability, structural integrity, recovery competence, and functional recovery, and conceptualizes recovery as a process involving not only metabolic reactivation but also reconstruction of functional organization. To characterize alternative outcomes following reversible arrest, we introduce the Cellular Recovery Landscape, while Recovery Information Integrity (RII) is proposed as a conceptual framework for the future quantitative operationalization of recovery-relevant organizational information. An important extension of SRIT is cytoskeletal–mechanical organization, which represents one of the most experimentally tractable potential substrates of SRI; actin and microtubule networks, motor proteins, crosslinkers, organelle positioning, and membrane–cytoskeleton interactions may provide spatial and mechanical constraints required for restoration of cellular architecture. On this basis, we propose the Cytoskeletal Recovery Scaffold (CRS) as a specific, testable example of a potential physical substrate of SRI. Within this framework, cellular recovery is viewed as constrained by the amount, integrity, and reconstructability of organizational information preserved during reversible cellular arrest. This perspective extends the problem of cellular recovery beyond desiccation and provides a unified conceptual framework for examining anhydrobiosis, hypometabolism, spores, seeds, cryopreservation, hibernation, anoxia, extreme cold, transient cellular arrest, stress-induced metabolic suppression, and cellular dormancy. SRIT therefore proposes that a cell should be understood not merely as a collection of preserved molecules, but as an organized system that must preserve sufficient information about its own architecture to regain a functional state.
